Lesson: Sing it, then Notate it

Sing an ending for a song three times. The computer works out which of the site’s familiar rhythm patterns and familiar tonal patterns you sang. Then you write it into the song on the Notation page, and it tells you when the rhythm is right and when the pitches are right.

The song

You sing an ending for Unfinished Song #1 from the tune library: its last two bars are empty, over V then I. The key, the tonality and the meter come from the song.

Sing it three times

Press Play and sing once. The song plays three times in a row without stopping. Each time, sing your ending in its last two bars, where only the chords play. Only those two bars are recorded. Sing every note on a syllable (“da”, “la”), and separate repeated notes.

What I heard

Nothing yet.

Notate it

Write what you sang in the song’s two empty bars: choose the rhythm patterns, then enter the notes with letters, the computer keys or a MIDI keyboard. The rhythm and the pitches are checked separately, each confirmed once. Octave does not matter for the pitches.

Sing three takes first.

How it works

  • Candidates. Rhythms come from the Rhythm Sequences bank (apps/rhythms/rhythm-pattern-object.js), bars of the chosen meter only; any two bars together make a candidate. Tonal patterns come from the Tonal Patterns bank (apps/patterns/pattern-object.js), the chosen tonality only, as semitones above the tonic, so the key does not change the match.
  • Your three takes (the song’s last two bars, each time round) are put on a sixteenth-note grid. A note counts when two takes agree on it. Your tuning drift (up to about a third of a semitone, sharp or flat all the way through) is removed.
  • The match. Every rhythm is scored by how well its onsets fit yours; the pitches are covered with as few tonal patterns as possible, in whichever octave you used. It is lenient: onsets count up to about a third of a beat early or late, a repeated note counts as one pitch of a pattern, a pattern’s notes count in any octave (5 down to 1 is the pattern 5 1), and held notes over whole beats (half notes) are familiar rhythms. A fit needs rhythm 66%, pitches 66% and the takes mostly in agreement. A note a half step out of the key never counts. Otherwise you get a warning and a chance to sing again, never a guess.
